user.name: Charley Dunkel
user.welcomeTitle: Charley's back, with a choice to make.
user.backstory: Charley fixed a bug in `app.py`, and also scribbled some messy notes in `notes.txt`. Only the bug fix should go in the next snapshot. Time to find out how Git lets you choose.

fields.label: Changed files
fields.value: app.py (a bug fix), notes.txt (personal notes, not ready to save)

cards.title: Git has three areas
body: Remember packing a box in Unit 1? Each step has a real name:
bullets: Working directory: the files on your laptop that you edit
Staging area: the box, holding the changes you picked for the next snapshot
Repository: your saved snapshots, kept in the hidden `.git` folder
cards.diagram: [ Working directory ]  --git add-->  [ Staging area ]  --git commit-->  [ Repository ]

cards.title: Why have a staging area?
body: The staging area lets you choose. If you changed two files but only one is ready, stage just that one. The snapshot will contain only what you put in the box.

cards.title: `git status` shows the areas
body: Now you know what red and green in `git status` really mean:
bullets: "Changes to be committed" (green): in the staging area
"Changes not staged for commit" (red): only in the working directory

cards.title: Taking something back out of the box
body: `git restore --staged notes.txt` takes a file out of the staging area but keeps your edits in the working directory.
Careful: don't mix it up with plain `git restore notes.txt` from Unit 2, which throws your edits away. The `--staged` makes all the difference.

questions.prompt: Charley picked some changes with `git add`. Which area are they in now?
questions.wrongFeedback: `git add` puts changes in the staging area, the box for the next snapshot. They reach the repository only after `git commit`.

questions.prompt: Only the bug fix is ready. Stage just `app.py`.
Charley changed their mind: the bug fix needs more work first. Take `app.py` back out of the staging area, without losing the edits.
After `git restore --staged app.py`, what happened to Charley's bug-fix edits?
options: They're still in the working directory, just not staged
They were saved in a snapshot
questions.wrongFeedback: `--staged` only takes the file out of the box. The edits are still in the working directory. (Plain `git restore` without `--staged` is the one that throws edits away.)

user.name: Jackson Stark
user.welcomeTitle: Jackson's back, and Charley has a question.
user.backstory: Charley messaged: "Which commit added the forecast? Send me its ID so I can take a look." Every commit has an ID, but what is it, and where does it come from?

cards.title: Snapshots, not lists of changes
body: Each commit is a snapshot: a picture of your whole project at that moment, not just a list of what changed. Files that didn't change aren't copied again. Git just points to the copy it already has. That's how Git stays fast and small.

cards.title: Every snapshot has an ID called a hash
body: Every commit gets an ID called a hash: 40 letters and numbers, like `4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2e3f...`. Git calculates it from everything in the commit: the files, the author, the time, the message, and the hash of the commit before it. Think of it as the commit's fingerprint.

cards.title: Why fingerprints matter
body: Change even one letter in a commit, and its hash changes completely. And because every commit includes the hash of the one before it, changing an old commit would change every hash after it too. So Git can always tell if history was changed.

cards.title: Using hashes
body: You usually only need the first 7 characters, like `4c5d6e7`. That's the short ID you saw with `git log --oneline` in Unit 2.
bullets: `git log` shows your commits with their full hashes
`git show 4c5d6e7` opens one snapshot and shows what changed in it

options: A password that protects the commit
A unique ID calculated from everything in the commit
questions.wrongFeedback: A hash is a commit's fingerprint: an ID Git calculates from the files, author, time, message and the commit before it.

questions.prompt: Show Jackson's commit history, with the full hashes.
Open the "Add 5-day forecast" snapshot using its short hash, `4c5d6e7`.
fakeOutput: +    # Get the weather for the next 5 days

questions.prompt: Someone secretly edits an old commit in Jackson's history. What happens to the hashes?
options: That commit's hash changes, and so does every hash after it
Only the newest commit's hash changes
questions.wrongFeedback: Each commit includes the hash of the one before it, so changing an old commit changes its hash and every hash after it.

user.name: Lily Lurvey
user.backstory: Lily has been saving snapshots for a while now, and even undid a broken commit. But where does Git actually keep all of that? Time to find Git's hidden database.

cards.title: Git is a database
body: A database is a place that stores information so you can look it up later. Git's database stores every snapshot of your project. It lives in a hidden folder called `.git` inside your project, created when you ran `git init`.
`ls -a` lists all files, including hidden ones (names starting with a dot). On Windows, use Git Bash for this.

cards.title: What's inside
body: Git stores three kinds of things:
bullets: File contents: what's inside each file
Folder lists: which files are in each folder
Commits: who, when, the message, and which snapshot came before
cards.footer: (If you're curious, their official names are blobs, trees and commits.)

cards.title: Everything is filed under its hash
body: Every item is stored under its hash, like a label on a drawer. Two files with exactly the same contents get the same hash, so Git stores them only once. That's why unchanged files aren't copied in every snapshot.

cards.title: Don't touch `.git`
body: Never edit or delete the `.git` folder yourself. If it's deleted, your current files stay, but every snapshot is gone: your whole history. (Unless it's also on GitHub. Another reason to push!)

questions.prompt: List all the files in Lily's project, including hidden ones.
Lily deletes the `.git` folder by accident (and never pushed). What's lost?
options: Every snapshot, the whole history. The current files stay.
The current files, but the history stays
questions.wrongFeedback: `.git` is the database. Delete it and every snapshot is gone, though the current files stay.

questions.prompt: Ask Git's database for all of Lily's snapshots, one per line.
Lily has two files with exactly the same contents. How many copies of those contents does Git store?
options: One, because same contents means the same hash
questions.wrongFeedback: Git files everything under its hash. Same contents, same hash, so it's stored only once.

user.name: Jackson Stark
user.backstory: Jackson, Charley and Lily are having a late study session at the library, when the Wi-Fi goes down. Lily panics: "Can we still work without GitHub?" Time to find out why Git says yes.

cards.title: Two ways to share a project
body: Centralized: one central server holds the history. Everyone's laptop only has the latest files. Older tools like Subversion (SVN) work this way.
Distributed: every copy has the full history. Git works this way.
cards.diagram:
Centralized:   [laptop]   [laptop]   [laptop]
                     \        |        /
               [ Server: the only history ]

Distributed:   [laptop: full history] <--> [GitHub: full history] <--> [laptop: full history]

cards.title: You already have everything
body: When you clone a project, you get every snapshot ever made, not just the latest files. That's why `git log`, `git commit`, `git branch` and `git switch` all work with no internet.

cards.title: Only some commands need internet
body: The commands that talk to GitHub need internet: `git clone`, `git push` and `git pull`. Everything else works anywhere, even on a plane.

cards.title: No single point of failure
body: In a centralized system, if the server breaks, the history can be lost. With Git, every clone is a full backup. GitHub is just the copy your team agreed to share. That's what "distributed" means.

questions.prompt: What's the big difference between centralized and distributed version control?
options: In distributed (like Git), every copy has the full history
questions.wrongFeedback: In a distributed system like Git, every copy has the full history. In a centralized one, only the server does.

questions.prompt: No Wi-Fi, so the push failed. But Jackson can still save new work. Commit the staged changes with the message on the profile card.

questions.prompt: The Wi-Fi is still down. Which of these commands won't work?
questions.wrongFeedback: `git push` talks to GitHub, so it needs internet. `git commit` and `git log` only use your own copy.

questions.prompt: Imagine GitHub's copy of the weather app was lost. Could the team get their project back?
options: No, GitHub had the only history
Yes, any teammate's clone has the full history
Only the latest files, not the history
questions.wrongFeedback: Every clone is a full copy of the history, so any teammate could put it all back.
